newsitem.title: USA: CIA knew 1961 Cuba invasion would fail - report.
newsitem.headline: CIA knew 1961 Cuba invasion would fail - report.

text.p: The chief CIA planner for the failed 1961 Cuba invasion knew the operation was doomed when President John Kennedy ordered the landing site changed a month before the invasion, a newspaper reported on Sunday.

Jack Hawkins, a retired Marine Corps colonel, said he knew "this plan had no chance" after he and his staff shifted the landing from a point near the city of Trinidad to the Bay of Pigs, about 80 miles (128 km) west on Cuba's south coast, the Miami Herald reported.
Planning for the military incursion known as the Bay of Pigs invasion began in January 1960 when the Eisenhower administration decided Fidel Castro should be removed.

The plan, continued under the Kennedy administration, evolved from a proposal to send teams of agents to develop resistance within Cuba into a full-scale landing at the Bay of Pigs by a Cuban exile brigade of about 1,500 in April 1961.

The landing ended in disaster when B-26 air strikes, reduced by Kennedy, failed to cripple Castro's air force. More than 100 of the invading brigade died and nearly 1,200 were captured by Castro's forces.
The Herald said its interview with Hawkins, conducted at his Fredericksburg, Virginia, home in December, was the first he had given to a daily newspaper since the invasion.

In the interview, Hawkins, 80, questioned Kennedy's commitment to the Cuba project and placed primary fault for its failure with the late Richard Bissell, the CIA's director of clandestine services who was in charge of the invasion.

Hawkins said he believed that failure became virtually inevitable a month before the invasion when Kennedy rejected the Trinidad landing as too "noisy," one that would attract too much attention to the United States.

"We were very surprised when we got word that the president had vetoed the Trinidad plan, which we thought was the best and probably only place in Cuba where we had a chance to pull this thing off," Hawkins told the Herald.
Hawkins said his staff determined the Bay of Pigs was the only alternate place that an airfield could be seized that would support B-26s, the Herald reported.
But Hawkins said he told Bissell that the site was wrong for the invasion because of its isolation and relative inaccessibility, the Herald said.

"After we got to drawing the detailed plan," Hawkins told the Herald, "I had time to do some careful thinking about the thing. Before, I had just been doing what I was told -- get a plan. So we got it. But then I decided this plan has no chance. It's going to fail."

Hawkins also said he learned only recently from declassified documents that Bissell had agreed with Kennedy to cut the number of CIA-supplied B-26 planes from 16, considered the minimum needed to knock out Castro's air force on the ground, to eight.
Hawkins said he did not learn of the reduction in air cover -- which he considered critical to any chance of success at the Bay of Pigs -- until the eve of the first air attack before the landing.
